content: Metrorrhagia refers to vaginal bleeding that occurs between a woman’s regular menstrual periods. This type of bleeding is also known as intermenstrual bleeding or spotting. Normal Menstrual Flow A typical menstrual period lasts about 4 days, with a variation of 2 to 3 days. The total blood loss during a normal period is approximately 30 to 80 milliliters. Menstrual cycles usually occur every 28 days, with a variation of 7 days. Abnormal Vaginal Bleeding Vaginal bleeding that occurs between periods or after menopause can have various causes. Most of these causes are benign and treatable. However, in some cases, abnormal bleeding may be due to cancer or precancerous conditions. Any unusual bleeding should be promptly evaluated by a healthcare provider. The risk of cancer increases to approximately 10% in women experiencing postmenopausal bleeding. It is important to confirm that the bleeding is coming from the vagina and not from the rectum or urine. Inserting a tampon can help identify the source of the bleeding, whether it is from the vagina, cervix, or uterus. A thorough examination by a healthcare provider is often the best way to determine the source of the bleeding. This examination can be performed even if you are actively bleeding, so do not delay seeking medical care. Causes of Metrorrhagia Uterine fibroids or cervical/uterine polyps Hormonal imbalances Cervical inflammation or infection (cervicitis) Injury or disease of the vaginal opening (caused by intercourse, infection, polyps, genital warts, ulcers, or varicose veins) Use of an intrauterine device (IUD), which may cause occasional spotting Ectopic pregnancy Miscarriage Other pregnancy-related complications Vaginal dryness due to low estrogen levels after menopause Stress Starting or stopping birth control pills or estrogen therapy Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) Use of blood thinners (anticoagulants) Cancer or precancerous conditions of the cervix, uterus, or, in rare cases, the fallopian tubes Cervical or endometrial biopsy or other medical procedures When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your healthcare provider if: You are pregnant. You experience unexplained bleeding between periods. You have any bleeding after menopause. You have heavy bleeding during your periods. Abnormal bleeding is accompanied by other symptoms, such as pain, fatigue, or dizziness. Diagnosis Your doctor will perform a physical examination and ask detailed questions about your medical history, with a focus on the pelvic area. Questions may include: Timing: When did the bleeding between periods begin? Does it occur consistently, such as every month? At what point in your menstrual cycle does the bleeding start? How long does the intermenstrual bleeding last? Quality: Is the bleeding heavy? How many tampons or pads are required? Are there cramps associated with the bleeding? Aggravating Factors: What makes the bleeding worse? Does physical activity or intercourse trigger the bleeding? Is stress associated with the bleeding? Relieving Factors: Does anything relieve or prevent the bleeding? Other Symptoms: Do you have abdominal pain or cramps? Is there increased bruising elsewhere on the body? Do you experience pain, burning, or difficulty with urination? Is there blood in your urine or stools? Additional Information: Are you pregnant? Have you had a miscarriage or abortion? Have you undergone a dilation and curettage (D&C) procedure? Have you ever had an abnormal Pap smear? What medications, hormones, or supplements are you taking? Are you using tampons? If so, what kind and size? At what age did your periods start? Have you had normal periods without intermenstrual bleeding in the past? Are you sexually active? Do you have a history of sexually transmitted infections? Are you using birth control? If so, what kind? Have you been injured? Have you received any medical or surgical treatments? Tests that may be performed include: Blood tests to evaluate thyroid and ovarian function Cervical cultures to check for sexually transmitted infections Colposcopy and cervical biopsy Endometrial (uterine) biopsy Pap smear Pelvic ultrasound Pregnancy test Home Care Contact a healthcare provider immediately if the bleeding is very heavy. Keep track of the number of pads or tampons used over time to help estimate the amount of blood loss. Note how frequently a pad or tampon is soaked and needs to be changed. Avoid aspirin if possible, as it may prolong bleeding. Where to Find Medical Care for Metrorrhagia Seek care from a qualified healthcare provider or gynecologist to address abnormal vaginal bleeding.
